name: Biology for Engineers
source: agent-written from the MANIT 2025-26 syllabus, NCERT class XI-XII biology (the book the seniors recommend for the topics taught) and standard first-year biology-for-engineers texts; importance is an ESTIMATE until past papers are imported
exam_notes: Set for non-biology students: mostly theory. Expect definitions and short notes (2-5 marks), 'differentiate between' tables (prokaryote/eukaryote, mitosis/meiosis, DNA/RNA, artery/vein, gene/cell therapy, in situ/ex situ), one or two 'describe the system with a labelled diagram' answers (5-10 marks) from human physiology, and process questions (rDNA steps, biosensor, bioprinting, biofuel generations) from Units 3-4; MCQs are likely in the mini test. Write from NCERT XI-XII and the class slides, draw neat labelled diagrams wherever a structure or process is named, and use tables for differences. The split by unit across mini (10), mid (20) and end term (40) is an estimate: usually the mid term covers the first one or two units and the end term the whole syllabus with more weight on Units 3-4.

topics.why: A near-certain 2-3 mark opener (postulates, who proposed what, exceptions); rarely more than 5 marks.
topics.gist:
The **cell theory** says the cell is the basic unit of structure and function of life. It was built in steps, and examiners like the names and dates:

- **Robert Hooke (1665)** saw dead cork "cells" and coined the word; **Leeuwenhoek** first saw living cells.
- **Matthias Schleiden (1838)**, a botanist, said all plants are made of cells; **Theodor Schwann (1839)**, a zoologist, said the same for animals and proposed the cell theory.
- Their version could not explain where new cells come from. **Rudolf Virchow (1855)** added *omnis cellula e cellula*: every cell arises from a pre-existing cell.

**Modern cell theory** adds that cells carry hereditary information (DNA) passed on during division, that all metabolism happens inside cells, and that cells of all organisms are basically alike in chemical composition.

Engineers should remember *why* cells are small: a cell exchanges material through its surface but needs it for its volume. For a sphere $SA/V = 3/r$, so doubling the radius halves the surface available per unit volume. That is the design limit that keeps most cells at 1-100 µm.

Know the **exceptions**: viruses (acellular, need a host cell), coenocytic/syncytial forms (*Rhizopus*, striated muscle fibres are multinucleate), and mature mammalian RBCs and sieve tubes (no nucleus, yet functional).
key_points: Hooke 1665 coined 'cell' from cork; Leeuwenhoek saw living cells (bacteria, sperm).
Schleiden 1838 (plants) and Schwann 1839 (animals); Schwann also described the plasma membrane and proposed the theory.
Virchow 1855: omnis cellula e cellula, cells arise from pre-existing cells.
Three classical postulates: all living organisms are made of cells and cell products; the cell is the basic unit of structure and function; new cells come from pre-existing cells.
Modern additions: DNA as hereditary material passed in division; energy flow/metabolism within cells; chemical similarity of all cells.
Size limit argument: surface area to volume ratio falls as the cell grows ($SA/V = 3/r$ for a sphere).
Exceptions: viruses, coenocytes/syncytia, enucleate RBCs and sieve tubes.
formulas: $\dfrac{SA}{V} = \dfrac{4\pi r^2}{\tfrac43 \pi r^3} = \dfrac{3}{r}$ — surface-to-volume ratio of a spherical cell
traps: Attributing 'cells arise from pre-existing cells' to Schleiden and Schwann: it is Virchow's.
Calling Hooke's observation 'living cells': he saw dead cork cell walls.
Listing viruses as cells; they are the standard exception.
Writing only three postulates when the question says 'modern cell theory'; add the DNA and metabolism points.
topics.asked_as: 'State the cell theory. Who modified it and how? (3 marks)'; 'Give two exceptions to the cell theory (2 marks)'; MCQs on names and dates in the mini test.

questions.q: Who proposed that every cell arises from a pre-existing cell?
questions.a: **Virchow (1855)**, *omnis cellula e cellula*. Schleiden and Schwann (1838-39) proposed the original theory but could not explain the origin of new cells.

questions.q: Which of the following is an exception to the cell theory?
questions.a: **Viruses** are acellular and can reproduce only inside a host cell, so they do not fit 'all living things are made of cells'. Amoeba, bacteria and yeast are single cells.

questions.q: State the postulates of the modern cell theory.
questions.a:
1. All living organisms are composed of one or more cells and cell products.
2. The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
3. All cells arise from pre-existing cells by division (Virchow).
4. Cells contain hereditary information (DNA) which is passed from cell to cell during division.
5. All metabolic reactions and energy flow of life occur within cells.
6. Cells of all organisms are basically similar in chemical composition.

questions.q: Distinguish the contributions of Schleiden, Schwann and Virchow to the cell theory.
questions.a:
- **Schleiden (1838, botanist):** all plants are composed of different kinds of cells which form plant tissues.
- **Schwann (1839, zoologist):** animal cells have a thin outer layer (plasma membrane); plant cells additionally have a cell wall; bodies of animals and plants are made of cells and their products. He proposed the cell theory (with Schleiden).
- **Virchow (1855):** new cells arise only from pre-existing cells (*omnis cellula e cellula*), completing the theory.

questions.q: Give three exceptions to the cell theory and say why each is an exception.
questions.a:
1. **Viruses:** acellular (nucleic acid in a protein coat), no metabolism of their own, multiply only inside a host cell.
2. **Coenocytic/syncytial organisms and tissues** (*Rhizopus*, *Vaucheria*, striated muscle fibres): many nuclei in a continuous cytoplasm, not divided into separate cells.
3. **Mature mammalian RBCs and phloem sieve tubes:** lack a nucleus yet perform their functions, so the 'cell carries DNA it passes on' idea does not hold for them.

questions.q: Two spherical cells have radii 5 µm and 20 µm. Compare their surface-area-to-volume ratios and explain what this means for the larger cell.
questions.a:
For a sphere $SA/V = 3/r$.

- $r = 5$ µm: $SA/V = 3/5 = 0.6\ \mu\text{m}^{-1}$
- $r = 20$ µm: $SA/V = 3/20 = 0.15\ \mu\text{m}^{-1}$

The larger cell has **one quarter** the surface per unit volume. Since nutrient uptake and waste removal occur across the membrane while demand scales with volume, the large cell cannot supply its interior fast enough by diffusion. This is why cells stay small, divide when they grow, or increase surface area (microvilli, flattened shapes).

topics.why: The most-asked 'draw a labelled diagram and explain' topic in Unit 1: mitochondria, ER/Golgi, lysosome, nucleus, membrane.
topics.gist:
A eukaryotic cell is a factory with departments, and the exam wants each department's **structure (what it looks like) and function (what it does)**, usually with a labelled diagram.

- **Plasma membrane:** lipid bilayer with proteins, the **fluid mosaic model** (Singer and Nicolson, 1972). Selectively permeable; transport is passive (diffusion, osmosis) or active (Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP).
- **Nucleus:** double membrane (nuclear envelope) with pores, chromatin, nucleolus (makes rRNA). Controls the cell and stores DNA.
- **Mitochondria:** double membrane, inner membrane folded into **cristae**, matrix with its own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes. Site of aerobic respiration and ATP: the *powerhouse*.
- **Chloroplast (plants):** double membrane, thylakoids stacked into grana, stroma; photosynthesis. Also has its own DNA, so both are *semi-autonomous* (endosymbiont origin).
- **Endomembrane system:** **RER** (ribosomes, protein synthesis), **SER** (lipids, steroids, detoxification), **Golgi** (cis face receives, trans face ships; packaging, glycosylation, forms lysosomes), **lysosomes** (acid hydrolases, pH about 5, autophagy, 'suicide bags'), vacuoles.
- **Ribosomes:** no membrane; 80S (60S + 40S) in eukaryotes, 70S (50S + 30S) in prokaryotes and organelles.
- Also: peroxisomes, centrosome/centrioles (9+0 triplets, spindle), cytoskeleton (microtubules, microfilaments), cilia/flagella (9+2), cell wall (plants: cellulose).
key_points: Fluid mosaic model: phospholipid bilayer, integral and peripheral proteins, lateral movement; selectively permeable.
Mitochondrion: outer and inner membranes, cristae, matrix, circular DNA, 70S ribosomes; Krebs cycle in matrix, ETS on inner membrane.
Chloroplast: thylakoids/grana (light reaction), stroma (Calvin cycle); semi-autonomous like mitochondria.
Endomembrane system = ER + Golgi + lysosomes + vacuoles (mitochondria, chloroplasts, peroxisomes are NOT part of it).
RER makes proteins for secretion/membranes; SER makes lipids and steroid hormones, detoxifies drugs.
Golgi: cis (forming) face toward ER, trans (maturing) face toward membrane; packages, modifies (glycoproteins, glycolipids), forms lysosomes.
Lysosome: hydrolytic enzymes active at acidic pH; intracellular digestion, autophagy, autolysis.
Ribosome: 80S = 60S + 40S; 70S = 50S + 30S; site of protein synthesis.
Nucleus: envelope with pores, nucleoplasm, chromatin, nucleolus (rRNA synthesis).
Centrioles 9+0 triplet microtubules; cilia/flagella axoneme 9+2.
traps: Adding Svedberg units: 60S + 40S gives 80S, not 100S, because S depends on shape as well as mass.
Putting mitochondria in the endomembrane system.
Saying lysosomes are 'made by ER': they bud from the Golgi (enzymes made on RER).
Diagram without labels or with cristae drawn on the outer membrane; marks are on the labels.
Saying prokaryotes have no ribosomes: they have 70S ribosomes, just no membrane-bound organelles.
topics.asked_as: 'Draw a labelled diagram of a mitochondrion and explain its function (5 marks)'; 'Write short notes on Golgi apparatus / lysosomes (3 marks)'; 'Explain the fluid mosaic model (5 marks)'; MCQs on 70S/80S and which organelle has DNA.

questions.q: Which pair of organelles contains its own DNA and 70S ribosomes?
questions.a: **Mitochondria and chloroplasts** carry circular DNA and 70S ribosomes and are called semi-autonomous; this supports the endosymbiotic theory.

questions.q: The 'suicide bags' of the cell are
questions.a: **Lysosomes**: membrane sacs of acid hydrolases (pH about 5). If the membrane ruptures the enzymes digest the cell itself (autolysis).

questions.q: A eukaryotic ribosome is made of subunits of
questions.a: **60S + 40S = 80S**. Svedberg units are not additive because sedimentation depends on shape and density as well as mass.

questions.q: Describe the structure of a mitochondrion with a labelled diagram and state its functions.
questions.a:
**Diagram (describe/draw):** an oval/sausage-shaped organelle, 0.2-1.0 µm wide and 1-4 µm long. Labels: **outer membrane** (smooth, porous), **intermembrane space**, **inner membrane** folded into **cristae**, **matrix**, **F₀-F₁ particles (oxysomes)** on the inner membrane, **circular DNA**, **70S ribosomes**.

**Structure:**
- Double membrane; the outer is permeable to small molecules (porins), the inner is selectively permeable and folded into cristae to increase area.
- Matrix contains enzymes of the Krebs cycle, circular DNA, RNA and 70S ribosomes, so it can make some of its own proteins (semi-autonomous).

**Functions:**
1. Site of aerobic respiration: Krebs cycle in the matrix, electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner membrane; produces most of the cell's **ATP** (powerhouse of the cell).
2. Makes some of its own proteins.
3. Involved in calcium storage, heat production (brown fat) and programmed cell death (apoptosis).
4. Divides by fission; inherited maternally.

questions.q: Explain the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane. What are the modes of transport across it?
questions.a:
**Fluid mosaic model (Singer and Nicolson, 1972):**
- The membrane is a **phospholipid bilayer**: hydrophilic heads face the aqueous outside and cytoplasm; hydrophobic tails face inward.
- **Proteins** are embedded like a mosaic: **integral** (span the bilayer, e.g. channels, carriers) and **peripheral** (on the surface).
- Cholesterol (animals) modulates fluidity; carbohydrates attached to proteins/lipids form glycoproteins/glycolipids (cell recognition).
- The bilayer is **fluid**: lipids and proteins move laterally, which allows cell growth, endocytosis, secretion and division.
- Human RBC membrane: about 52% protein, 40% lipid.

**Transport:**
1. **Passive** (no energy, down the gradient): simple diffusion (O₂, CO₂), osmosis (water), facilitated diffusion through channel/carrier proteins (glucose).
2. **Active** (uses ATP, against the gradient): e.g. **Na⁺/K⁺ pump** moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP.
3. **Bulk transport:** endocytosis (phagocytosis, pinocytosis) and exocytosis.

questions.q: Write short notes on the Golgi apparatus.
questions.a:
- Discovered by **Camillo Golgi (1898)**. Stack of flattened, disc-shaped **cisternae** (0.5-1.0 µm), with vesicles.
- **Polarity:** the **cis (forming) face** faces the ER and receives vesicles; the **trans (maturing) face** faces the plasma membrane and releases vesicles.
- **Functions:** packaging and dispatch of materials to intracellular targets or outside the cell; site of **glycosylation**, forming glycoproteins and glycolipids; forms **lysosomes** and secretory vesicles; makes the cell plate in plant cell division.
- Part of the endomembrane system, working with the ER.

questions.q: Distinguish between rough ER and smooth ER.
questions.a:
| Rough ER | Smooth ER |
|---|---|
| Ribosomes on its surface | No ribosomes |
| Mostly cisternae | Mostly tubules |
| Protein synthesis and secretion | Lipid and steroid synthesis |
| Abundant in protein-secreting cells (pancreas) | Abundant in steroid-secreting and liver cells (detoxification) |
| Continuous with outer nuclear membrane | Usually continuous with RER |

topics.why: 'Differentiate between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells' (and plant vs animal cell) is one of the surest 3-5 mark questions in the paper.
topics.gist:
Cells come in two basic designs.

**Prokaryotic cells** (bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma, archaea) are small (1-10 µm) and simple: no membrane-bound nucleus (DNA lies in a **nucleoid**), no membrane-bound organelles, **70S ribosomes**, a cell wall of **peptidoglycan** in bacteria, often extra **plasmids**, and **mesosomes** (infoldings of the membrane). They divide by binary fission. A bacterial cell envelope has glycocalyx, cell wall and plasma membrane; Gram-positive walls are thick, Gram-negative walls thin with an outer membrane.

**Eukaryotic cells** (protists, fungi, plants, animals) are larger (10-100 µm) with a true nucleus, membrane-bound organelles, **80S ribosomes**, linear chromosomes with histones, and mitosis/meiosis.

Within eukaryotes, **plant cells** have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts, a large central vacuole, and usually no centrioles; **animal cells** have no wall, small vacuoles, centrioles and lysosomes.

The syllabus also uses 'cell types' for **specialised cells** in the body (neurons, muscle, epithelial, blood cells: shape follows function) and **stem cells**: *totipotent* (zygote, can form a whole organism), *pluripotent* (embryonic stem cells, any cell type), *multipotent* (adult stem cells such as haematopoietic). Stem cells link this topic to cell therapy and tissue engineering in Units 3 and 4.
key_points: Prokaryote: nucleoid, no nuclear membrane, no membrane organelles, 70S ribosomes, circular DNA without histones, plasmids, binary fission.
Eukaryote: true nucleus, membrane organelles, 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes, linear DNA with histones, mitosis/meiosis.
Bacterial cell wall = peptidoglycan (murein); fungi = chitin; plants = cellulose.
Gram-positive (thick peptidoglycan, retain crystal violet) vs Gram-negative (thin wall + outer membrane, LPS).
Plant vs animal cell: wall, plastids, large vacuole in plants; centrioles, lysosomes common in animals.
Stem cell potency: totipotent > pluripotent > multipotent > unipotent.
Specialised cells: shape follows function (neuron long processes, RBC biconcave, muscle contractile fibres).
traps: Saying prokaryotes have no ribosomes or no DNA.
Calling mitochondria present in prokaryotes; respiration happens on the plasma membrane/mesosome.
A 'difference' table with only one column filled, or points that are not paired; each row must contrast the same feature.
Calling viruses prokaryotes.
Saying all plant cells have chloroplasts (root cells do not).
topics.asked_as: 'Differentiate between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells (any five points) (5 marks)'; 'Differentiate plant and animal cells (3 marks)'; 'What are stem cells? Classify them by potency (3 marks)'.

questions.q: Which of the following is found in a prokaryotic cell?
questions.a: Prokaryotes have **70S ribosomes** but no membrane-bound organelles or nuclear envelope.

questions.q: Embryonic stem cells that can form any cell type of the body but not a whole organism are
questions.a: **Pluripotent.** Only the zygote and very early blastomeres are totipotent (can also form extra-embryonic tissues and a whole organism); adult stem cells are multipotent.

questions.q: Differentiate between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells (any eight points).
questions.a:
| Feature | Prokaryotic cell | Eukaryotic cell |
|---|---|---|
| Size | 1-10 µm | 10-100 µm |
| Nucleus | No nuclear envelope; nucleoid | True nucleus with envelope and nucleolus |
| DNA | Circular, naked (no histones) | Linear, with histones (chromatin) |
| Membrane-bound organelles | Absent | Present (mitochondria, ER, Golgi, etc.) |
| Ribosomes | 70S (50S + 30S) | 80S (60S + 40S) in cytoplasm |
| Cell wall | Peptidoglycan (bacteria) | Cellulose (plants), chitin (fungi), absent in animals |
| Plasmids | Commonly present | Rare (yeast 2µ plasmid) |
| Cell division | Binary fission | Mitosis and meiosis |
| Respiration site | Plasma membrane / mesosomes | Mitochondria |
| Examples | Bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycoplasma | Protists, fungi, plants, animals |

questions.q: Differentiate between plant and animal cells.
questions.a:
| Plant cell | Animal cell |
|---|---|
| Cellulose cell wall present | No cell wall |
| Plastids (chloroplasts) present | Absent |
| Large central vacuole | Small, temporary vacuoles |
| Centrioles usually absent | Centrioles present |
| Cytokinesis by cell plate | Cytokinesis by furrowing |
| Reserve food starch | Reserve food glycogen |
| Usually rectangular/fixed shape | Usually rounded/irregular |

questions.q: Draw and label a typical bacterial cell.
questions.a:
**Labels:** glycocalyx/capsule (outermost), **cell wall** (peptidoglycan), **plasma membrane**, **mesosome** (infolding of membrane: wall formation, DNA replication, respiration), cytoplasm with **70S ribosomes**, **nucleoid** (circular DNA), **plasmid**, inclusion bodies, **flagellum** (basal body, hook, filament), **pili/fimbriae**.

The cell envelope is the three layers glycocalyx, wall and membrane acting as one protective unit. No nuclear membrane or membrane-bound organelles should be drawn.

questions.q: What are stem cells? Explain totipotent, pluripotent and multipotent stem cells with examples.
questions.a:
**Stem cells** are undifferentiated cells that can **self-renew** (divide to make more stem cells) and **differentiate** into specialised cells.

- **Totipotent:** can form all cells of the body and extra-embryonic tissues, i.e. a whole organism. Example: zygote, blastomeres up to the 8-cell stage.
- **Pluripotent:** can form any cell of the three germ layers but not a whole organism. Example: embryonic stem cells from the inner cell mass; induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs).
- **Multipotent:** can form a limited family of related cells. Example: haematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow (all blood cells), mesenchymal stem cells (bone, cartilage, fat).

topics.why: 'Differentiate between mitosis and meiosis' and 'describe the stages of mitosis with diagrams' appear in almost every first-year biology paper.
topics.gist:
A cell grows, copies its DNA and divides: the **cell cycle**. A human cell in culture takes about 24 h; yeast about 90 min.

**Interphase (about 95% of the time):** **G₁** (growth, normal metabolism), **S** (DNA replication: content goes from 2C to 4C but chromosome number stays 2n), **G₂** (proteins for mitosis, organelle duplication). Cells that stop dividing enter **G₀** (quiescent; e.g. neurons, heart muscle). **Checkpoints** at G₁/S, G₂/M and metaphase stop the cycle if DNA is damaged; failure of these controls gives **cancer**.

**Mitosis (equational division)** produces two identical diploid cells: **prophase** (chromatin condenses, spindle forms, nuclear envelope and nucleolus disappear), **metaphase** (chromosomes on the metaphase plate, best stage to study morphology), **anaphase** (centromeres split, sister chromatids move to opposite poles), **telophase** (nuclear envelopes reform), then **cytokinesis** (furrow in animals, cell plate in plants). Role: growth, repair, asexual reproduction.

**Meiosis (reductional division)** in germ cells gives four haploid cells. **Meiosis I** halves the chromosome number; its long **prophase I** has leptotene, zygotene (**synapsis**, synaptonemal complex), pachytene (**crossing over**, recombination nodules), diplotene (**chiasmata**), diakinesis. Homologues separate in anaphase I. **Meiosis II** is like mitosis. Role: keeps chromosome number constant across generations and creates variation.

Engineers can treat bacterial growth as a geometric series: $N = N_0 2^{n}$.
key_points: Cell cycle phases: G₁, S, G₂ (interphase), M; G₀ = quiescent stage.
S phase doubles DNA (2C → 4C), chromosome number unchanged (2n).
Mitosis stages: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase; cytokinesis separate.
Metaphase: chromosomes aligned at equator, kinetochores attached to spindle fibres.
Anaphase: centromere splits, chromatids move to poles.
Meiosis I reductional (homologues separate), meiosis II equational (chromatids separate).
Prophase I substages: leptotene, zygotene (synapsis), pachytene (crossing over), diplotene (chiasmata), diakinesis (terminalisation).
Significance of meiosis: constant chromosome number across generations, genetic variation via crossing over and independent assortment.
Checkpoints and cancer: loss of control gives uncontrolled division.
formulas: $N = N_0 \cdot 2^{n}$ — cells after $n$ divisions (binary fission or mitosis)
$n = \dfrac{t}{g}$ — number of generations in time $t$ with generation time $g$
$2n \xrightarrow{\text{meiosis}} 4 \times n$ — one diploid cell gives four haploid cells
traps: Saying chromosome number doubles in S phase: DNA doubles, chromosome number does not.
Saying crossing over happens in zygotene or diplotene: it occurs in **pachytene**; chiasmata become visible in diplotene.
Mixing up meiosis I and II: homologues separate in anaphase I, sister chromatids in anaphase II.
Calling interphase a 'resting phase' without saying it is metabolically very active.
Diagrams of mitosis without labels for spindle, centromere, chromatids.
topics.asked_as: 'Differentiate between mitosis and meiosis (5 marks)'; 'Describe the stages of mitosis with neat diagrams (5-10 marks)'; 'Explain prophase I of meiosis (5 marks)'; 'What is G₀? (2 marks)'; MCQs on stage identification.

questions.q: Crossing over between non-sister chromatids takes place during
questions.a: **Pachytene.** Synapsis is in zygotene; chiasmata (the visible sites of crossing over) are seen in diplotene.

questions.q: A cell has 2C DNA and 2n chromosomes in G₁. After S phase it has
questions.a: **4C and 2n.** Replication doubles the DNA, but each chromosome now has two sister chromatids joined at one centromere, so the chromosome count is unchanged.

questions.q: The best stage to count chromosomes and study their morphology is
questions.a: **Metaphase**: chromosomes are maximally condensed and aligned at the equatorial plate.

questions.q: Differentiate between mitosis and meiosis.
questions.a:
| Feature | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Occurs in | Somatic cells | Germ cells (gonads, spore mother cells) |
| Divisions | One | Two (meiosis I and II) |
| Daughter cells | Two | Four |
| Chromosome number | Unchanged (2n → 2n), equational | Halved (2n → n), reductional |
| Synapsis / crossing over | Absent | Present in prophase I |
| Prophase | Short, simple | Long, five substages in prophase I |
| Anaphase | Sister chromatids separate | Anaphase I: homologues separate; anaphase II: chromatids |
| Genetic make-up | Daughters identical to parent | Daughters genetically different |
| Role | Growth, repair, asexual reproduction | Gamete formation, variation, constant chromosome number across generations |

questions.q: Describe the stages of mitosis with labelled diagrams.
questions.a:
**Prophase:** chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, each of two sister chromatids joined at a centromere; centrosome duplicates and the centrioles move to opposite poles, forming the spindle; nucleolus, Golgi and ER disappear; nuclear envelope breaks down by the end. *Diagram:* condensed chromosomes, asters at the poles.

**Metaphase:** spindle fibres attach to the **kinetochores**; chromosomes align on the **metaphase (equatorial) plate**. *Diagram:* chromosomes in a line at the equator, spindle fibres to both poles.

**Anaphase:** centromeres split; sister chromatids (now daughter chromosomes) move to opposite poles, centromere leading, arms trailing (V/J shapes). *Diagram:* two sets moving apart.

**Telophase:** chromosomes reach the poles and decondense; nuclear envelope, nucleolus, Golgi and ER reform around each set. *Diagram:* two nuclei forming.

**Cytokinesis:** animals form a **cleavage furrow** that deepens and pinches the cell in two; plants form a **cell plate** (from Golgi vesicles) from the centre outward, which becomes the middle lamella.

**Significance:** growth, repair and regeneration, maintains the same chromosome number, asexual reproduction, restores nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio.

questions.q: A bacterium has a generation time of 20 minutes. Starting from 100 cells under ideal conditions, how many cells are there after 2 hours?
questions.a:
Number of generations $n = t/g = 120/20 = 6$.

$N = N_0 \cdot 2^{n} = 100 \times 2^{6} = 100 \times 64 = 6400$ cells.

questions.q: What is the G₀ phase? Give examples of cells in G₀.
questions.a:
**G₀ (quiescent stage)** is a stage cells enter when they exit G₁ and stop dividing. They remain metabolically active and do their normal work but do not proliferate unless signalled (some can re-enter G₁).

Examples: **neurons** and **cardiac muscle cells** (permanently in G₀); **liver cells** (can re-enter the cycle after injury); lymphocytes until antigen stimulation.

topics.why: Every paper has a classification-of-biomolecules question and a short note on a metabolic or genetic disorder (diabetes, PKU, sickle cell, lactose intolerance).
topics.gist:
Living matter is mostly water plus four families of **biomolecules**:

- **Carbohydrates** $(\mathrm{CH_2O})_n$: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose), disaccharides (sucrose, lactose, maltose) joined by **glycosidic bonds**, polysaccharides (starch, glycogen as storage; cellulose, chitin as structure). Energy source.
- **Proteins**: polymers of 20 amino acids joined by **peptide bonds**; four levels of structure (primary sequence, secondary α-helix/β-sheet, tertiary fold, quaternary subunits like haemoglobin). Enzymes, transport, structure, hormones, antibodies.
- **Lipids**: fats and oils (glycerol + 3 fatty acids = triglyceride via ester bonds), phospholipids (membranes), steroids (cholesterol). Not true polymers.
- **Nucleic acids**: DNA and RNA, polymers of nucleotides (sugar + phosphate + base) joined by **phosphodiester bonds**.

**Enzymes** are protein catalysts that lower activation energy; they are specific and sensitive to temperature, pH and inhibitors, with kinetics $v = V_{max}[S]/(K_m+[S])$.

When a biomolecule's synthesis or breakdown fails we get **disorders**:
- **Diabetes mellitus**: high blood glucose; Type 1 no insulin (autoimmune β-cell loss), Type 2 insulin resistance.
- **Phenylketonuria (PKU)**: autosomal recessive lack of phenylalanine hydroxylase; phenylalanine accumulates, damaging the brain.
- **Sickle-cell anaemia**: autosomal recessive; Glu → Val at position 6 of β-globin (GAG → GUG); HbS polymerises at low O₂.
- **Lactose intolerance**: lactase deficiency; undigested lactose fermented in the colon gives gas and diarrhoea.
key_points: Bonds: glycosidic (sugars), peptide (amino acids), ester (lipids), phosphodiester (nucleotides).
Starch (amylose + amylopectin) and glycogen store energy; cellulose and chitin are structural.
Protein structure: primary, secondary (α-helix, β-sheet; H-bonds), tertiary, quaternary.
DNA vs RNA: deoxyribose vs ribose; thymine vs uracil; double vs usually single strand; genetic material vs protein synthesis roles.
Chargaff's rule for dsDNA: A = T, G = C, purines = pyrimidines; A=T two H-bonds, G≡C three.
Enzymes: specificity, active site, lock-and-key / induced fit, effect of temperature and pH, competitive inhibition (malonate on succinate dehydrogenase).
Diabetes Type 1 vs Type 2; symptoms polyuria, polydipsia, glycosuria.
PKU: phenylalanine hydroxylase deficient; mental retardation; phenylpyruvic acid in urine; controlled by low-phenylalanine diet.
Sickle cell: single base substitution GAG → GUG, Glu → Val at 6th position of β chain; heterozygote carriers resistant to malaria.
Lactose intolerance: deficient lactase; bloating, diarrhoea after milk.
formulas: $v = \dfrac{V_{max}[S]}{K_m + [S]}$ — Michaelis-Menten enzyme kinetics; $K_m$ is $[S]$ at $v = V_{max}/2$

questions.q: Write short notes on (a) diabetes mellitus and (b) lactose intolerance.
questions.a:
**(a) Diabetes mellitus** is a metabolic disorder with chronically high blood glucose (fasting ≥ 126 mg/dL) due to lack of insulin or its action.
- **Type 1 (insulin-dependent, juvenile):** autoimmune destruction of pancreatic β-cells of the islets of Langerhans; little or no insulin; treated with insulin injections (recombinant human insulin).
- **Type 2 (non-insulin-dependent, adult onset):** cells become resistant to insulin; linked to obesity and inactivity; diet, exercise, oral drugs.
- **Symptoms:** glycosuria (glucose in urine), polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, weight loss; ketone bodies in severe cases.
- **Complications:** damage to kidneys, eyes (retinopathy), nerves and blood vessels.

**(b) Lactose intolerance** is the inability to digest **lactose** (milk sugar) because of deficiency of the enzyme **lactase** (β-galactosidase) in the small intestine. Lactose is not split into glucose and galactose, passes to the colon, and is fermented by bacteria, producing gas, bloating, cramps and diarrhoea. It is common in adults (lactase production declines after weaning). Managed by avoiding milk, using lactose-free milk or lactase supplements; curd is better tolerated.

questions.q: Classify carbohydrates with examples and give their functions.
questions.a:
Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, general formula $(\mathrm{CH_2O})_n$.

1. **Monosaccharides** (cannot be hydrolysed further): trioses (glyceraldehyde), pentoses (ribose, deoxyribose), hexoses (glucose, fructose, galactose). Glucose is the main fuel.
2. **Disaccharides** (two monosaccharides by a glycosidic bond): sucrose = glucose + fructose; lactose = glucose + galactose; maltose = glucose + glucose.
3. **Oligosaccharides**: 3-10 units (raffinose).
4. **Polysaccharides**:
   - *Storage*: **starch** (plants; amylose + amylopectin; forms blue colour with iodine because I₂ sits in its helix), **glycogen** (animals, liver and muscle; highly branched).
   - *Structural*: **cellulose** (plant cell wall; β-1,4 glucose; no helix, no iodine colour), **chitin** (fungal walls, arthropod exoskeleton; N-acetylglucosamine).

**Functions:** energy source and store, structural support, components of nucleic acids (ribose, deoxyribose), cell recognition (glycoproteins).

topics.why: A standard 10-mark 'describe the human digestive system with a labelled diagram' question; enzyme tables are favourite short answers.
topics.gist:
Digestion turns large insoluble food molecules into small soluble ones that can be absorbed. Learn it as a **pipe with glands**.

**Alimentary canal:** mouth (buccal cavity, teeth, tongue) → pharynx → oesophagus → **stomach** (cardiac, fundic, pyloric parts) → **small intestine** (duodenum, jejunum, ileum) → **large intestine** (caecum with vermiform appendix, colon, rectum) → anus. The wall has four layers: serosa, muscularis, submucosa, mucosa. Food moves by **peristalsis**.

**Glands and their work:**
- **Salivary glands** (parotid, submandibular, sublingual): salivary amylase (ptyalin) begins starch → maltose (about 30% of starch digested in the mouth); lysozyme kills bacteria.
- **Gastric glands**: chief/peptic cells give **pepsinogen** (activated by HCl to pepsin, proteins → peptones); parietal/oxyntic cells give **HCl** (pH about 1.8) and intrinsic factor (vitamin B₁₂ absorption); mucus cells. **Rennin** curdles milk in infants.
- **Liver** (largest gland): **bile**, which has no enzymes but **emulsifies fats**.
- **Pancreas**: trypsinogen (activated by **enterokinase** to trypsin), chymotrypsinogen, pancreatic amylase, lipase, nucleases.
- **Intestinal glands** (succus entericus): maltase, sucrase, lactase, dipeptidases, lipases, nucleotidases complete digestion.

**Absorption** is mainly in the small intestine, whose **villi and microvilli** give a huge area. Sugars and amino acids go to blood capillaries; fats as **chylomicrons** into **lacteals** (lymph). The large intestine absorbs water and some minerals. Hormones gastrin, secretin, CCK coordinate it. Disorders: jaundice, diarrhoea, constipation, indigestion, vomiting.
key_points: Parts of alimentary canal in order, with three parts of small intestine and of large intestine.
Dental formula of adult human: 2123/2123 (32 teeth; thecodont, diphyodont, heterodont).
Salivary amylase: starch → maltose at pH 6.8.
Gastric juice: HCl, pepsinogen → pepsin, rennin (infants), mucus, intrinsic factor.
Bile: bile salts emulsify fats; no digestive enzymes.
Pancreatic juice: trypsinogen activated by enterokinase; amylase, lipase, nucleases.
Succus entericus completes digestion: disaccharidases, dipeptidases.
Villi and microvilli increase absorptive area; lacteals absorb fats as chylomicrons.
Hormonal control: gastrin, secretin, cholecystokinin (CCK), GIP.
Disorders: jaundice (liver, bile pigments), diarrhoea, constipation, indigestion.
traps: Saying bile contains lipase or digests fats: it only emulsifies them.
Writing that pepsin is secreted directly: it is secreted as inactive pepsinogen and activated by HCl.
Confusing enterokinase (intestinal enzyme activating trypsinogen) with trypsin.
Diagram without the liver, gall bladder and pancreas with their ducts opening into the duodenum.
Saying most absorption happens in the stomach; only water, simple sugars, alcohol, some drugs are absorbed there.

questions.q: Describe the human digestive system with a neat labelled diagram.
questions.a:
**Diagram labels:** mouth/buccal cavity, salivary glands, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, liver, gall bladder, bile duct, pancreas and pancreatic duct, duodenum, jejunum, ileum, caecum, vermiform appendix, ascending/transverse/descending colon, rectum, anus.

**Alimentary canal:**
1. **Mouth:** teeth (mastication), tongue (mixing, taste), saliva (salivary amylase: starch → maltose; lysozyme).
2. **Pharynx and oesophagus:** swallowing; peristalsis carries the bolus to the stomach.
3. **Stomach:** J-shaped; gastric glands secrete HCl (kills microbes, acid pH), pepsinogen → pepsin (proteins → peptones), rennin (curdles milk in infants), mucus. Food becomes **chyme**.
4. **Small intestine:** duodenum (receives bile and pancreatic juice), jejunum and ileum (digestion completed by succus entericus; absorption through villi and microvilli).
5. **Large intestine:** caecum, colon, rectum; absorbs water and minerals, forms faeces, bacteria make some vitamins; defecation through the anus.

**Digestive glands:**
- **Liver:** bile (bile salts emulsify fats, bile pigments bilirubin/biliverdin are excretory), stored in the gall bladder.
- **Pancreas:** exocrine juice with trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, amylase, lipase, nucleases; endocrine islets make insulin and glucagon.
- **Intestinal glands:** maltase, sucrase, lactase, dipeptidases, lipases, nucleosidases.

**Absorption and assimilation:** monosaccharides and amino acids enter blood capillaries and reach the liver via the hepatic portal vein; fats enter lacteals as chylomicrons. Absorbed nutrients are used by tissues (assimilation).

**Control:** gastrin (stomach acid), secretin and CCK (pancreatic juice and bile).

questions.q: What is the role of bile in digestion?
questions.a:
- Bile is made by the **liver** and stored in the **gall bladder**; it reaches the duodenum through the common bile duct.
- It has **no digestive enzymes**.
- **Bile salts** emulsify fats into tiny droplets, increasing surface area for lipase, and help absorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) by forming micelles.
- Makes the medium alkaline, neutralising acid chyme.
- Bile pigments (bilirubin, biliverdin) are excreted through it; their build-up causes **jaundice**.

questions.q: How is the small intestine adapted for absorption?
questions.a:
1. Very long (about 6 m) with folds of the mucosa.
2. **Villi** (finger-like projections) and **microvilli** (brush border) give an enormous surface area.
3. Each villus has a dense **capillary network** (for sugars, amino acids) and a central **lacteal** (for fats).
4. Thin epithelium (one cell thick) for short diffusion distance.
5. Active transport and facilitated diffusion carriers in the epithelial membranes.

topics.why: Mechanism of breathing, lung volumes and O₂/CO₂ transport are asked as 5-10 mark questions; numericals on vital capacity appear.
topics.gist:
Respiration here means **breathing and gas exchange**: getting O₂ to the tissues and removing CO₂.

**Pathway:** external nostrils → nasal chamber (filters, warms, moistens) → pharynx → **larynx** (voice box; the epiglottis stops food entering) → **trachea** (C-shaped cartilage rings keep it open) → primary bronchi → secondary/tertiary bronchi → bronchioles → terminal bronchioles → **alveoli**. The conducting part ends at terminal bronchioles; the exchange part is the alveoli. Lungs sit in a double-layered **pleural** sac.

**Mechanism (Boyle's law at work):** in **inspiration** the diaphragm contracts and flattens and the external intercostal muscles lift the ribs and sternum; thoracic volume rises, intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric, air flows in. **Expiration** at rest is passive: muscles relax, volume falls, pressure rises, air flows out.

**Volumes:** tidal volume (TV) about 500 mL; IRV 2500-3000 mL; ERV 1000-1100 mL; residual volume 1100-1200 mL. Vital capacity = TV + IRV + ERV; total lung capacity = VC + RV.

**Exchange** is by simple diffusion driven by partial pressure: alveolar pO₂ 104 mmHg vs 40 in deoxygenated blood; pCO₂ 40 vs 45. CO₂ is about 20-25 times more soluble, so a smaller gradient suffices. **Transport:** about 97% of O₂ as **oxyhaemoglobin**, 3% dissolved; CO₂ about 70% as **bicarbonate** (carbonic anhydrase in RBCs), 20-25% as carbaminohaemoglobin, 7% dissolved. The **oxygen dissociation curve** is sigmoid; high pCO₂, H⁺ and temperature shift it right (Bohr effect), releasing O₂ in tissues. Breathing is controlled by the medulla's respiratory rhythm centre (with pneumotaxic centre in pons).
key_points: Respiratory passage order from nostrils to alveoli; conducting vs exchange part.
Inspiration active (diaphragm + external intercostals); normal expiration passive.
Lung volumes: TV 500 mL, IRV 2500-3000, ERV 1000-1100, RV 1100-1200 mL.
Capacities: VC = TV + IRV + ERV; TLC = VC + RV; FRC = ERV + RV; IC = TV + IRV.
Partial pressures (mmHg): alveolus O₂ 104 / CO₂ 40; deoxygenated blood O₂ 40 / CO₂ 45; oxygenated blood O₂ 95 / CO₂ 40.
O₂ transport: 97% as oxyhaemoglobin; each Hb carries up to 4 O₂; 100 mL oxygenated blood delivers about 5 mL O₂ to tissues.
CO₂ transport: 70% bicarbonate, 20-25% carbamino, 7% dissolved; carbonic anhydrase; chloride shift.
Oxygen dissociation curve sigmoid; right shift with ↑pCO₂, ↑H⁺, ↑temperature (Bohr effect).
Control: medulla respiratory rhythm centre, pneumotaxic centre in pons, chemosensitive area sensitive to CO₂ and H⁺.

questions.q: Explain the mechanism of breathing in humans.
questions.a:
Breathing moves air by creating a **pressure gradient** between the lungs and the atmosphere (Boyle's law: at constant temperature, pressure ∝ 1/volume).

**Inspiration (active):**
1. The **diaphragm** contracts and flattens, increasing the thoracic volume in the antero-posterior axis.
2. The **external intercostal muscles** contract, lifting the ribs and sternum outward and upward, increasing volume in the dorso-ventral axis.
3. Increased thoracic volume increases pulmonary volume; intra-pulmonary pressure falls below atmospheric.
4. Air flows in until the pressures equalise.

**Expiration (normally passive):**
1. Diaphragm and external intercostals relax; the diaphragm domes up and ribs return.
2. Thoracic and pulmonary volumes decrease; intra-pulmonary pressure rises slightly above atmospheric.
3. Air is expelled.

**Forced breathing:** additional muscles in the abdomen and internal intercostals increase the strength of inspiration and expiration.

A healthy adult breathes 12-16 times per minute, moving about 6-8 L of air per minute.

questions.q: Describe the transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide in blood.
questions.a:
**Oxygen:**
- About **97%** bound to haemoglobin in RBCs as **oxyhaemoglobin**; about **3%** dissolved in plasma.
- Binding depends mainly on **pO₂**; also pCO₂, H⁺ and temperature. A plot of % saturation vs pO₂ is the **sigmoid oxygen dissociation curve**.
- In the alveoli (high pO₂, low pCO₂, low H⁺, lower temperature) Hb loads O₂; in tissues (low pO₂, high pCO₂, high H⁺, higher temperature) it unloads. This rightward shift in tissues is the **Bohr effect**.
- Every 100 mL of oxygenated blood delivers about 5 mL of O₂ to tissues under normal conditions.

**Carbon dioxide:**
- About **20-25%** as **carbaminohaemoglobin** (CO₂ binds Hb; favoured by high pCO₂ and low pO₂ in tissues).
- About **70%** as **bicarbonate**: in RBCs, **carbonic anhydrase** catalyses $\mathrm{CO_2 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_2CO_3 \rightleftharpoons HCO_3^- + H^+}$; HCO₃⁻ moves to plasma in exchange for Cl⁻ (**chloride shift**). The reaction reverses in the lungs, releasing CO₂.
- About **7%** dissolved in plasma.
- Every 100 mL of deoxygenated blood delivers about 4 mL of CO₂ to the alveoli.

questions.q: Describe the human respiratory system with a labelled diagram.
questions.a:
**Diagram labels:** external nostrils, nasal chamber, pharynx, larynx with epiglottis, trachea with cartilaginous rings, right and left primary bronchi, secondary/tertiary bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli (inset), lungs, pleural membranes, ribs and intercostal muscles, diaphragm.

**Conducting part** (nostrils to terminal bronchioles): transports air, **filters** it (hairs, mucus, cilia), **warms and humidifies** it.
1. **Nostrils and nasal chamber:** hair and mucus trap dust; rich blood supply warms the air.
2. **Pharynx:** common passage for food and air.
3. **Larynx (sound box):** cartilaginous; the **epiglottis** (elastic cartilage flap) covers the glottis during swallowing.
4. **Trachea:** straight tube to the mid-thorax, kept open by incomplete **C-shaped cartilage rings**; ciliated mucous lining.
5. **Bronchi and bronchioles:** trachea divides at the 5th thoracic vertebra into right and left primary bronchi, which branch repeatedly into secondary, tertiary bronchi and bronchioles ending in terminal bronchioles.

**Exchange (respiratory) part:** **alveoli**, very thin, irregular-walled, vascularised bag-like structures; the site of diffusion of O₂ and CO₂ between air and blood.

**Lungs:** two, covered by a double-layered **pleura** with pleural fluid that reduces friction. The thoracic chamber is air-tight, formed by the vertebral column, sternum, ribs and the **diaphragm** below; changes in its volume drive breathing.

**Steps of respiration:** breathing (ventilation) → diffusion across the alveolar membrane → transport of gases by blood → diffusion between blood and tissues → cellular use of O₂.

topics.why: The nephron diagram with urine formation (filtration, reabsorption, secretion) is close to certain in the mid or end term, often for 10 marks.
topics.gist:
Excretion removes nitrogenous wastes. Animals are **ammonotelic** (ammonia: bony fish), **ureotelic** (urea: mammals, amphibians) or **uricotelic** (uric acid: birds, reptiles). Humans are ureotelic; urea is made in the liver (ornithine cycle) and removed by the kidneys.

**Organs:** two kidneys → ureters → urinary bladder → urethra. Each kidney has an outer **cortex** and inner **medulla** (renal pyramids), and about **one million nephrons**.

**Nephron:** the **glomerulus** (capillary tuft between a wider **afferent** and a narrower **efferent arteriole**) sits in **Bowman's capsule**; together they are the **Malpighian body/renal corpuscle**. Then the **PCT** (proximal convoluted tubule), **loop of Henle** (descending and ascending limbs), **DCT**, which opens into the **collecting duct**. The efferent arteriole forms the peritubular capillaries and the **vasa recta**. Cortical nephrons have short loops; juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops.

**Urine formation:**
1. **Glomerular filtration (ultrafiltration):** blood pressure pushes plasma minus proteins into Bowman's capsule. GFR is about 125 mL/min, i.e. 180 L/day.
2. **Tubular reabsorption:** about 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed. PCT reabsorbs most glucose, amino acids, Na⁺ and water; descending limb permeable to water only; ascending limb permeable to electrolytes only.
3. **Tubular secretion:** H⁺, K⁺, NH₃ secreted, maintaining pH and ion balance.

The **counter-current mechanism** (loop of Henle and vasa recta) builds a medullary osmolarity gradient from 300 to 1200 mOsm/L so urine can be concentrated. **Regulation:** ADH (water reabsorption), the **renin-angiotensin-aldosterone** system (JGA senses low GFR), ANF (opposes RAAS). About 1-1.5 L of urine per day. Disorders: uraemia, renal failure (haemodialysis), renal calculi, glomerulonephritis.
key_points: Ammonotelic, ureotelic, uricotelic with examples.
Kidney structure: cortex, medulla, pyramids, pelvis, hilum, columns of Bertini.
Nephron parts in order: glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct.
Afferent arteriole wider than efferent: keeps glomerular pressure high for filtration.
GFR about 125 mL/min (180 L/day); urine about 1.5 L/day; about 99% reabsorbed.
Filtration through three layers: capillary endothelium, basement membrane, podocytes with filtration slits.
PCT: reabsorbs nearly all glucose, amino acids, 70-80% electrolytes and water; descending limb water-permeable; ascending limb impermeable to water.
Counter-current: loop of Henle + vasa recta; NaCl and urea maintain medullary gradient 300 → 1200 mOsm/L.
Regulation: ADH, RAAS (JGA, renin, angiotensin II, aldosterone), ANF.
Dialysis: blood passed through a semipermeable membrane against dialysing fluid without nitrogenous wastes; heparin as anticoagulant.

$C_x = \dfrac{U_x \dot V}{P_x}$ — renal clearance of substance $x$ (inulin clearance = GFR)

Saying the descending limb is permeable to salts and the ascending limb to water: it is the reverse.

questions.a: **About 125 mL/min**, i.e. about 180 L of filtrate a day, of which about 99% is reabsorbed.

Ascending limb of loop of Henle

questions.q: Draw a labelled diagram of a nephron and explain the mechanism of urine formation.
questions.a:
**Diagram labels:** afferent arteriole, glomerulus, efferent arteriole, Bowman's capsule, proximal convoluted tubule, descending limb, loop of Henle, ascending limb, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct, peritubular capillaries, vasa recta; mark cortex and medulla.

**1. Glomerular filtration:** the afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent, so glomerular hydrostatic pressure is high. Blood is filtered through the glomerular endothelium, basement membrane and podocyte filtration slits into Bowman's capsule. The filtrate is plasma without proteins. GFR about 125 mL/min (180 L/day). The JGA regulates GFR.

**2. Tubular reabsorption:** about 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed.
- **PCT:** simple cuboidal brush-border epithelium; reabsorbs nearly all glucose and amino acids, 70-80% of electrolytes and water; secretes H⁺, NH₃, K⁺; keeps pH and ionic balance.
- **Descending limb:** permeable to water, almost impermeable to electrolytes; filtrate becomes concentrated.
- **Ascending limb:** impermeable to water, transports electrolytes out; filtrate becomes dilute.
- **DCT:** conditional reabsorption of Na⁺ and water (aldosterone, ADH); secretion of H⁺, K⁺; reabsorption of HCO₃⁻.
- **Collecting duct:** reabsorbs large amounts of water under ADH to give concentrated urine; lets some urea into the medulla to keep the osmotic gradient.

**3. Tubular secretion:** H⁺, K⁺, ammonia and some drugs are secreted into the filtrate, maintaining acid-base and ionic balance.

**Concentration:** the counter-current flow in the loop of Henle and vasa recta keeps a medullary gradient from 300 mOsm/L (cortex) to 1200 mOsm/L (inner medulla), so water leaves the collecting duct and urine can be up to four times as concentrated as the filtrate. About 1-1.5 L of urine is passed daily.

questions.q: Explain the counter-current mechanism in the kidney.
questions.a:
- The two limbs of the **loop of Henle** carry filtrate in opposite directions, and the **vasa recta** also form a hairpin with blood flowing in opposite directions: a **counter-current** arrangement.
- The **ascending limb** pumps NaCl out into the medullary interstitium but is impermeable to water. The **descending limb** is permeable to water, so water leaves it into the salty interstitium and the filtrate becomes concentrated toward the tip.
- **Urea** leaving the inner collecting duct also adds to the interstitial osmolarity and is partly recycled into the thin ascending limb.
- The vasa recta carry NaCl and water away slowly in the counter-current pattern, so the gradient is not washed out.
- Result: medullary interstitial osmolarity increases from **300 mOsm/L** in the cortex to about **1200 mOsm/L** in the inner medulla.
- In the presence of **ADH** the collecting duct becomes permeable to water, which leaves into this hypertonic medulla, giving concentrated urine and conserving water.

questions.q: What is haemodialysis and when is it used?
questions.a: When kidneys fail, urea accumulates in blood (**uraemia**). In **haemodialysis** blood is taken from a convenient artery, mixed with an anticoagulant (**heparin**), and pumped through a dialyser where it flows past a cellophane-like **semipermeable membrane** bathed in **dialysing fluid** that has the same composition as plasma except for nitrogenous wastes. Urea and other wastes diffuse out down their concentration gradient; the cleaned blood gets anti-heparin and is returned through a vein. Kidney transplantation is the permanent solution.

questions.q: A person's GFR is 125 mL/min and urine output is 1.5 L/day. What percentage of the filtrate is reabsorbed?
questions.a:
Filtrate per day $= 125\ \text{mL/min} \times 1440\ \text{min} = 180{,}000\ \text{mL} = 180$ L.

Reabsorbed $= 180 - 1.5 = 178.5$ L.

Percentage $= \dfrac{178.5}{180} \times 100 \approx 99.2\%$.

topics.why: Asked as a 5-10 mark 'describe the human skeleton / types of joints' question; bone counts are favourite MCQs.
topics.gist:
The adult human skeleton has **206 bones**, divided into the **axial skeleton (80)** along the body's axis and the **appendicular skeleton (126)** of limbs and girdles.

**Axial (80):** skull 29 (cranium 8, face 14, hyoid 1, ear ossicles 6: malleus, incus, stapes ×2), vertebral column 26 (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 1 sacrum, 1 coccyx), sternum 1, ribs 24 (12 pairs: 7 true, 3 false, 2 floating).

**Appendicular (126):** each forelimb 30 (humerus, radius, ulna, 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges), each hind limb 30 (femur, tibia, fibula, patella, 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges), pectoral girdle 4 (clavicle and scapula each side), pelvic girdle 2 (coxal bones of ilium, ischium, pubis).

**Bone as a material:** a composite of about two-thirds mineral (**hydroxyapatite**, $\mathrm{Ca_{10}(PO_4)_6(OH)_2}$) for stiffness and one-third **collagen** for toughness. Compact bone is built of **Haversian systems** (osteons); spongy bone has trabeculae. **Osteoblasts** build, **osteoclasts** resorb, **osteocytes** maintain. **Cartilage** is avascular connective tissue (hyaline, elastic, fibrous).

**Joints:** **fibrous** (immovable, skull sutures), **cartilaginous** (slightly movable, between vertebrae, pubic symphysis), **synovial** (freely movable, fluid-filled cavity): ball-and-socket (shoulder, hip), hinge (knee, elbow), pivot (atlas-axis), gliding (between carpals), saddle (carpal-metacarpal of thumb).

**Functions:** support, protection, movement with muscles (levers), blood cell formation in red marrow, mineral store. Disorders: **osteoporosis**, **arthritis**, **gout** (uric acid crystals in joints), myasthenia gravis and muscular dystrophy (muscle).

Vertebral column 26: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, sacrum (5 fused), coccyx (4 fused).
Ribs: 7 pairs true (vertebrosternal), 3 pairs false (vertebrochondral), 2 pairs floating.
Limb bones 30 each; girdles: pectoral 4, pelvic 2.
Bone composition: hydroxyapatite + collagen; compact (Haversian system) vs spongy bone.
Cells: osteoblasts (formation), osteoclasts (resorption), osteocytes (maintenance).
Joint types: fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial (ball-and-socket, hinge, pivot, gliding, saddle) with examples.
Disorders: osteoporosis, arthritis, gout.

Counting the hyoid and ear ossicles outside the skull total; NCERT counts the skull as 29 bones including them.
Calling the knee a ball-and-socket joint: it is a hinge (modified).
Confusing osteoporosis (loss of bone mass) with osteoarthritis (joint cartilage wear) and gout (uric acid).
Saying cartilage has blood vessels.

questions.q: Classify joints in the human body with examples.
questions.a:
Joints are points of contact between bones, or between bones and cartilage. Classified by structure and mobility:

1. **Fibrous joints (synarthroses):** bones joined by dense fibrous connective tissue; no movement. Example: **sutures** of the skull.
2. **Cartilaginous joints (amphiarthroses):** bones joined by cartilage; limited movement. Example: joints between adjacent **vertebrae** (intervertebral discs), pubic symphysis.
3. **Synovial joints (diarthroses):** a fluid-filled **synovial cavity** between articulating surfaces, enclosed in a capsule; ends covered with articular cartilage; free movement.
   - **Ball-and-socket:** shoulder (humerus-pectoral girdle), hip (femur-acetabulum); movement in all planes.
   - **Hinge:** knee, elbow; movement in one plane.
   - **Pivot:** atlas-axis; rotation.
   - **Gliding:** between carpals, between tarsals; sliding.
   - **Saddle:** carpal-metacarpal joint of the thumb; two planes.
   - (Condyloid/ellipsoid: wrist, between radius and carpals.)

questions.q: Describe the structure of compact bone.
questions.a:
- Compact bone is made of repeating units called **Haversian systems (osteons)**.
- Each has a central **Haversian canal** carrying blood vessels and nerves, surrounded by concentric **lamellae** of hard matrix.
- **Lacunae** between lamellae contain **osteocytes**, connected by fine **canaliculi** for nutrient exchange.
- **Volkmann's canals** run transversely, linking Haversian canals and the periosteum.
- The matrix is collagen fibres mineralised with calcium phosphate (hydroxyapatite), giving strength in compression and some toughness.

questions.q: Write short notes on osteoporosis and gout.
questions.a:
**Osteoporosis:** age-related disorder with **decreased bone mass** and increased fracture risk. Common cause: decreased oestrogen after menopause; also low calcium/vitamin D, inactivity. Bones become porous and brittle (hip, spine, wrist fractures).

**Gout:** inflammation of joints due to deposition of **uric acid crystals**, from excess production or reduced excretion of uric acid. Typically the big toe; painful, red, swollen joint.

topics.why: Heart structure with cardiac cycle and double circulation is a near-certain 10-mark question; artery vs vein and ECG are standard short answers.
topics.gist:
The circulatory system has **blood** (plasma 55%, formed elements 45%: RBCs, WBCs, platelets), **vessels** and the **heart**.

**Heart:** in the pericardium, four chambers: two thin-walled **atria** and two thick-walled **ventricles** (left wall thickest; it pumps to the whole body). Valves: **tricuspid** (right AV), **bicuspid/mitral** (left AV), **semilunar** valves at the pulmonary artery and aorta; they ensure one-way flow. Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles stop AV valves from everting.

**Conduction (myogenic heart):** **SA node** (pacemaker, 70-75 impulses/min, right atrium wall) → atria contract → **AV node** (delay) → **bundle of His** → bundle branches → **Purkinje fibres** → ventricles contract from apex upward.

**Cardiac cycle (about 0.8 s at 72 beats/min, NCERT):** atrial systole about 0.1 s (tops up ventricles by about 30%), ventricular systole about 0.3 s (AV valves close: **'lub'**, first heart sound; semilunar valves open, blood ejected), joint diastole about 0.4 s (semilunar valves close: **'dub'**, second sound; ventricles fill passively). Stroke volume about 70 mL, so **cardiac output** $= 72 \times 70 \approx 5$ L/min.

**ECG:** **P** wave = atrial depolarisation, **QRS** = ventricular depolarisation (start of ventricular systole), **T** = ventricular repolarisation.

**Double circulation:** pulmonary (right ventricle → lungs → left atrium) and systemic (left ventricle → body → right atrium). Hepatic portal system and coronary circulation are special paths. Normal BP 120/80 mmHg. Disorders: hypertension, coronary artery disease (atherosclerosis), angina, heart failure.

First sound 'lub' = AV valves close; second sound 'dub' = semilunar valves close.
Stroke volume about 70 mL; cardiac output about 5 L/min.
ECG waves P, QRS, T and what each means.
Double circulation: pulmonary and systemic; no mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in mammals.
Artery vs vein: thick vs thin walls, away from vs toward heart, valves only in veins, high vs low pressure.
Blood groups ABO and Rh; clotting cascade (thrombokinase, prothrombin → thrombin, fibrinogen → fibrin).

$SV = EDV - ESV$ — stroke volume from end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes
$EF = \dfrac{SV}{EDV}$ — ejection fraction (normally about 55-70%)
$T_{cycle} = \dfrac{60}{HR}\ \text{s}$ — duration of one cardiac cycle

Mixing up the heart sounds: 'lub' is AV closure at the start of ventricular systole.
Saying the AV node is the pacemaker.
Calling the T wave atrial repolarisation; atrial repolarisation is hidden in the QRS.
Writing that the right ventricle has the thickest wall.

questions.q: Describe the structure of the human heart and explain the cardiac cycle.
questions.a:
**Structure (diagram labels):** pericardium, right and left atria, right and left ventricles, interatrial and interventricular septa, tricuspid valve, bicuspid (mitral) valve, pulmonary and aortic semilunar valves, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles, superior and inferior vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, aorta, SA node, AV node, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres.

- Mesodermal, in the thoracic cavity between the lungs, in a double-walled **pericardium** with pericardial fluid.
- Four chambers: thin-walled atria receive blood; thick-walled ventricles pump it (left thickest).
- Valves prevent backflow: tricuspid (right atrium → right ventricle), bicuspid (left atrium → left ventricle), semilunar valves at the exits.
- **Nodal tissue** makes the heart **myogenic**: SA node (pacemaker) → AV node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibres.

**Cardiac cycle** (one heartbeat, about 0.8 s at 72 bpm):
1. **Joint diastole (start):** all chambers relaxed; AV valves open, semilunar valves closed; blood flows from veins through atria into ventricles.
2. **Atrial systole (about 0.1 s):** SA node fires; atria contract, increasing ventricular filling by about 30%.
3. **Ventricular systole (about 0.3 s):** impulse via AV node and bundle of His; ventricles contract, pressure rises, **AV valves close (first sound 'lub')**; then **semilunar valves open** and blood is ejected into the pulmonary artery and aorta.
4. **Ventricular diastole:** ventricles relax, pressure falls, **semilunar valves close (second sound 'dub')**; when ventricular pressure falls below atrial, AV valves open and filling resumes. Joint diastole lasts about 0.4 s.

Each ventricle ejects about **70 mL (stroke volume)**; cardiac output $= HR \times SV \approx 5$ L/min.

questions.q: Differentiate between arteries and veins.
questions.a:
| Artery | Vein |
|---|---|
| Carries blood away from the heart | Carries blood toward the heart |
| Oxygenated blood (except pulmonary artery) | Deoxygenated blood (except pulmonary veins) |
| Thick, elastic, muscular walls | Thin, less elastic walls |
| Narrow lumen | Wide lumen |
| No valves | Valves present to prevent backflow |
| Blood under high pressure, flows in spurts | Low pressure, smooth flow |
| Usually deep-seated | Many superficial |
| Does not collapse when empty | Collapses when empty |

questions.q: A person's heart rate is 75 beats/min, end-diastolic volume 120 mL and end-systolic volume 50 mL. Find the stroke volume, cardiac output, ejection fraction and duration of one cardiac cycle.
questions.a:
- $SV = EDV - ESV = 120 - 50 = 70$ mL
- $CO = HR \times SV = 75 \times 70 = 5250$ mL/min $= 5.25$ L/min
- $EF = SV/EDV = 70/120 \approx 0.58 = 58\%$
- $T_{cycle} = 60/HR = 60/75 = 0.8$ s

questions.q: What is double circulation? Why is it important?
questions.a:
Blood passes **twice through the heart** for one complete circuit of the body:
- **Pulmonary circulation:** right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs (oxygenation) → pulmonary veins → left atrium.
- **Systemic circulation:** left ventricle → aorta → arteries → tissues → veins → venae cavae → right atrium.

**Importance:** oxygenated and deoxygenated blood never mix (complete septation), so tissues get fully oxygenated blood; pressures can differ (low in lungs, high in body), giving efficient high-pressure supply needed by warm-blooded, high-energy animals.

topics.why: Neuron diagram, nerve impulse and the reflex arc are standard 5-10 mark questions; CNS parts give short answers.
topics.gist:
The nervous system detects, integrates and responds, fast and point-to-point.

**Organisation:** **CNS** (brain and spinal cord) and **PNS** (cranial and spinal nerves). PNS fibres are **afferent** (sensory, to CNS) or **efferent** (motor, from CNS). The efferent part is **somatic** (voluntary, skeletal muscle) or **autonomic** (involuntary: sympathetic for fight-or-flight, parasympathetic for rest-and-digest).

**Neuron:** a **cell body (cyton)** with nucleus and **Nissl's granules**, branched **dendrites** (bring impulses in), a long **axon** (takes them away) ending in **synaptic knobs** with neurotransmitter vesicles. Myelinated axons have a **myelin sheath** from **Schwann cells** with gaps called **nodes of Ranvier**. Types: multipolar (cerebral cortex), bipolar (retina), unipolar (embryo).

**Nerve impulse:** at rest the membrane is **polarised**: about **−70 mV** inside, kept by the **Na⁺/K⁺ pump** (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in) and higher K⁺ permeability. A stimulus opens Na⁺ channels; Na⁺ rushes in (**depolarisation**, inside becomes about +30 mV, the **action potential**). K⁺ channels then open and K⁺ leaves (**repolarisation**). The wave propagates along the axon; in myelinated fibres it jumps node to node (**saltatory conduction**, much faster).

**Synapse:** electrical (rare, fast) or chemical: the impulse releases a neurotransmitter (e.g. **acetylcholine**) into the synaptic cleft; it binds receptors on the post-synaptic membrane and opens ion channels.

**Brain:** forebrain (cerebrum with cortex and corpus callosum; thalamus; hypothalamus controlling temperature, hunger, hormones), midbrain, hindbrain (pons, **cerebellum** for balance and coordination, **medulla** for breathing, heart rate, BP).

**Reflex arc:** receptor → sensory neuron (dorsal root) → spinal cord (interneuron) → motor neuron (ventral root) → effector.
key_points: CNS vs PNS; afferent vs efferent; somatic vs autonomic (sympathetic, parasympathetic).
Neuron parts: cyton, Nissl's granules, dendrites, axon, myelin sheath, Schwann cell, node of Ranvier, synaptic knob.
Neuron types: multipolar, bipolar, unipolar; myelinated vs non-myelinated.

Action potential: Na⁺ influx (depolarisation), K⁺ efflux (repolarisation); all-or-none; refractory period.
Saltatory conduction in myelinated fibres is faster.
Chemical synapse: neurotransmitter release, binding, ion channel opening; acetylcholine.
Brain regions and functions: cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, pons, cerebellum, medulla.

Placing the sensory neuron in the ventral root: sensory = dorsal root, motor = ventral root.
Saying reflexes are controlled by the brain: they are mediated by the spinal cord (spinal reflexes).

questions.a: Voltage-gated **Na⁺ channels open and Na⁺ rushes in**, making the inside positive. K⁺ efflux follows during repolarisation.

questions.a: Sensory (afferent) fibres enter via the **dorsal root** (cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion); motor fibres leave via the ventral root.

questions.q: Draw a labelled diagram of a myelinated neuron and explain how a nerve impulse is generated and conducted.
questions.a:
**Diagram labels:** dendrites, cell body (cyton), nucleus, Nissl's granules, axon hillock, axon, myelin sheath, Schwann cell, node of Ranvier, axon terminal, synaptic knob.

**Resting potential:** the axonal membrane is more permeable to K⁺ than Na⁺, and the **Na⁺/K⁺ pump** moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP. So the outside is positive and the inside negative (about **−70 mV**): the membrane is **polarised**.

**Generation (action potential):** a stimulus at a point makes the membrane freely permeable to **Na⁺**; Na⁺ rushes in and the inside becomes positive (about +30 mV) relative to outside: **depolarisation**. This is all-or-none once threshold is reached.

**Repolarisation:** Na⁺ channels close and **K⁺ channels open**; K⁺ diffuses out, restoring the negative inside. The pump restores the ion distribution. During the refractory period the region cannot fire again, so the impulse moves one way.

**Conduction:** local currents from the depolarised site depolarise the adjacent membrane, so the wave travels along the axon. In **myelinated** fibres the myelin insulates, so depolarisation occurs only at the **nodes of Ranvier**: the impulse jumps from node to node (**saltatory conduction**), which is faster and uses less energy.

**Transmission at the synapse:** at the axon terminal, Ca²⁺ entry triggers release of neurotransmitter (e.g. acetylcholine) into the synaptic cleft; it binds receptors on the post-synaptic membrane, opening ion channels and generating a new potential.

questions.q: What is a reflex action? Explain the reflex arc with a diagram.
questions.a:
A **reflex action** is a rapid, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus, mediated by the spinal cord (or brain stem) without conscious thought, e.g. withdrawing a hand from a hot object, knee-jerk.

**Reflex arc** (pathway of a reflex), diagram of a transverse section of the spinal cord with:
1. **Receptor** (in skin/muscle) detects the stimulus.
2. **Afferent (sensory) neuron** carries the impulse to the spinal cord through the **dorsal root**; cell body in the dorsal root ganglion.
3. **Integration centre** in the grey matter of the spinal cord: an **interneuron** (relay neuron) in polysynaptic reflexes; in the **knee-jerk** the sensory neuron synapses directly with the motor neuron (monosynaptic).
4. **Efferent (motor) neuron** leaves through the **ventral root**.
5. **Effector** (muscle/gland) produces the response.

Significance: speed, protection from injury, relieves the brain of routine work.

questions.q: Give the functions of cerebrum, cerebellum, hypothalamus and medulla oblongata.
questions.a:
- **Cerebrum:** intelligence, memory, thinking, voluntary movement, sensory perception (cortex: motor, sensory and association areas); corpus callosum connects the hemispheres.
- **Cerebellum:** coordination of movement, balance and posture.
- **Hypothalamus:** controls body temperature, hunger, thirst, urge for eating and drinking; produces neurohormones regulating the pituitary.
- **Medulla oblongata:** controls involuntary functions: respiration, heart rate, blood pressure, swallowing, coughing, vomiting.

questions.q: Differentiate between sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems.
questions.a:
| Sympathetic | Parasympathetic |
|---|---|
| Prepares body for emergency ('fight or flight') | Restores rest ('rest and digest') |
| Increases heart rate and BP | Decreases heart rate and BP |
| Dilates pupils and bronchioles | Constricts pupils and bronchioles |

topics.why: The bridge topic between biology and engineering; examiners set one 5-mark 'explain the heart as a pump / kidney as a filter' question, but it varies by teacher and this is the least predictable topic in Unit 2.
topics.gist:
An engineer can model each organ as a device with inputs, outputs and limits.

**Heart as a pump:** a pair of synchronised positive-displacement pumps with check valves (AV and semilunar valves). Output: $CO = HR \times SV \approx 5$ L/min at rest, up to 20-25 L/min in exercise. Each beat does work $W = \oint P\,dV$ (area of the **pressure-volume loop**), about 1 J for the left ventricle. Vessels are a hydraulic circuit: $\Delta P = Q \cdot R$ (the fluid analogue of Ohm's law) with resistance from **Poiseuille's law** $R = 8\eta L/(\pi r^4)$, so halving a vessel's radius raises resistance 16 times, which is why atherosclerosis matters.

**Lungs as a gas exchanger:** a huge, thin membrane (alveolar area about 70 m², barrier about 0.5 µm) obeying **Fick's law** $J \propto A\,\Delta p/T$. The **law of Laplace** $P = 2\gamma/r$ explains why small alveoli would collapse without **surfactant**.

**Kidney as a filter:** ultrafiltration driven by pressure difference (net filtration pressure about 10 mmHg), selective by size and charge, then a counter-current exchanger that concentrates urine. Dialysers are counter-current membrane mass exchangers.

**Bones as structures:** a composite beam/column; stress $\sigma = F/A$, Young's modulus $E = \sigma/\varepsilon$ (cortical bone about 15-20 GPa); **Wolff's law**: bone remodels to the loads it carries, which also causes **stress shielding** around stiff implants.

**Nerves as signalling cables:** electrochemical signals, resting potential from ion gradients (Nernst), insulation by myelin raising conduction speed, digital (all-or-none) coding by frequency. Homeostasis is **negative feedback control**.
key_points: Heart: two pumps in series, valves as check valves; CO = HR × SV; P-V loop area = stroke work.
Circulation as hydraulic circuit: ΔP = Q × R; Poiseuille resistance ∝ 1/r⁴.
Lungs: Fick's diffusion law; large area (about 70 m²), thin barrier; Laplace law and surfactant.
Kidney: pressure-driven ultrafilter plus counter-current concentrator; dialyser as engineered analogue.
Bone: composite material, stress, strain, Young's modulus; Wolff's law; stress shielding.
Joints as bearings; synovial fluid as lubricant with very low friction coefficient.
Nerve: electrochemical cable; myelin as insulator; saltatory conduction; all-or-none digital coding.
Biosignals: ECG (heart), EEG (brain), EMG (muscle) used in diagnostics and myoelectric prostheses.
Homeostasis as a negative feedback control loop: sensor, controller, effector (e.g. thermoregulation, blood glucose).

$W_{stroke} = \oint P\,dV \approx MAP \times SV$ — stroke work from the pressure-volume loop
$\Delta P = Q R$, $R = \dfrac{8 \eta L}{\pi r^4}$ — hydraulic analogue of Ohm's law with Poiseuille resistance
$J = D \dfrac{A\,\Delta p}{T}$ — Fick's law of diffusion across the alveolar membrane
$P = \dfrac{2\gamma}{r}$ — law of Laplace for an alveolus (sphere, surface tension $\gamma$); smaller $r$ needs more pressure to stay open
$\sigma = \dfrac{F}{A},\ \varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L},\ E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}$ — stress, strain and Young's modulus for bone

Saying resistance is proportional to $1/r^2$: Poiseuille's law gives $1/r^4$.
Forgetting units: CO in L/min, pressures in mmHg, modulus in GPa.
Treating nerve conduction like current in a copper wire: it is propagated regeneration of membrane potential, much slower (up to about 120 m/s).
